criterion_notes.c1: Chapters 1 to 3 establish that the dissertation examines community and household domestic water supply sources located in micro spring forests on Ukerewe main Island, Tanzania, including natural spring wells and HESAWA-improved spring systems equipped with tanks, pipes, and taps from which rural households fetch domestic water.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the study clearly examines institutional, governance, legal-pluralism, and customary/statutory tenure factors in rural water management (so plain Criterion 2 = yes, though overall plain_criterion2_decision remains cannot_tell because all empirical chapters are truncated). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, eligibility is unclear from the provided excerpt: Chapters 1 to 4 and the Table of Contents point to potentially qualifying rule-type mechanisms—including water users' registers in five of six sites (p. 33), Table 5.5 on HESAWA rules (p. 80), Ukerewe District Council administrative formalization of HESAWA activities (p. 82), bureaucratic barriers to registering Water User Associations/Groups and enacting village by-laws (p. 54), and Section 7.2 on ownership and control of access and use of water sources (pp. 113-118)—but because the text is truncated at PDF Page 69 of 216 (printed p. 55), we cannot verify whether these mechanisms are empirically analysed as rules directly governing household service access (e.g., registration/eligibility screening, user fees/cost recovery, tenure-based exclusion, or enforcement sanctions) rather than cultural taboos and forest vegetation conservation.
criterion_notes.c3: Chapter 3 (PDF Pages 41-55, pp. 27-41) documents primary mixed-methods empirical fieldwork conducted in 2006-2008 across six micro spring forest water sources in four villages, combining PRA, ethnographic interviews and observation, physical water-source and forest inventory measurements, and a random survey of 180 households (Table 3.3 reports survey respondent demographics), alongside policy/legal tenure analysis in Chapter 4. However, the empirical findings chapters (Chapters 5-8) are in the truncated portion of the file.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear due to truncation at PDF Page 69 of 216: Chapter 3 (p. 40) and the List of Tables (pp. x-xi) indicate that the thesis measured relevant household and source-level water-access outcomes—including daily household water quantity fetched (Table 7.5, p. 127), functional status of water taps, tanks, and pipes (Table 5.6, p. 86), seasonal water quantity and flow rates (Table 5.8, p. 89), control of access and use (Section 7.2, p. 118), factors affecting water-source use (Table 7.6, p. 128), and use of alternative water sources (Table 7.7, p. 130)—but none of these empirical outcome sections are visible in the provided text.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (180 randomly sampled households—30 per site—across 6 water sources in 4 villages on Ukerewe main Island, plus source/community cases) and study design (comparative mixed-methods case study) are identifiable in Chapter 3. However, because Chapters 5-8 and the thesis summaries (PDF Pages 70-216) are truncated, we cannot verify how institutional/rule-type exposures are empirically linked to water-access outcomes (note that the linear regression described on p. 40 lists physical distance, household size, alternative sources, and dependence as independent variables, while institutional effects on access control and use in Sections 5.2 and 7.2-7.3 are cut off).
criterion_notes.c6: The dissertation is written in English (with summaries noted in English, Dutch, and Kiswahili).

evidence_quotes.quote: The term micro spring forests refers to forest patches with the average size ranging from 0.1 to 1 ha surrounding natural water sources. These natural wells are used by villagers for collecting water for domestic uses, and the small streams deriving from these springs are used for local irrigation.

The improvement of traditional water sources by HESAWA programme considers these water sources as lacking proper management and technological facilities to improve water quality. The programme introduced water tanks, taps, well committees and Water User Groups to ensure sustainability of these water sources.

Water users’ registers for Tumbu, Kilombero, Chemichemi, Anselm and Migombani water sources were used to select the respondents for the surveys. Nzuitaka had no register for water users so the households using this water source were grouped into three zones.
The current study in Ukerewe main Island shows that there are no registered Water User Associations or Water User Groups (see Chapter 7 on the organization of water use).

A linear regression analysis was used to show the relationship between the amount of water fetched by households per day (dependent variable) and the distance from the water source, household size, the presence of alternative water sources and the dependence on water source (independent variables).

raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural households and water users across six micro spring forest water sources (Nzuitaka, Tumbu, Kilombero, Chemichemi, Anselm, and Migombani) in four villages (Mahande, Bwassa, Busiri, and Bugula) on Ukerewe main Island, Ukerewe District, Tanzania; N=180 randomly sampled households (30 per case) plus key informants and PRA groups
raw_response.rationale: The retrieved document matches the metadata (Katani 2010 Wageningen PhD dissertation on micro spring forests and water sources in Ukerewe, Tanzania), but the provided full text is truncated at PDF Page 69 of 216 (printed p. 55, mid-Chapter 4), omitting all empirical results chapters (Chapters 5, 6, 7, and 8) as well as the thesis Summary (pp. 189-192). From Chapters 1-4 and the Table of Contents, the study clearly examines rural household/community domestic water sources (including HESAWA-improved spring wells with tanks, pipes, taps, and water users' registers in five of six sites) using a mixed-methods comparative case study and household survey (N=180). However, without Chapters 5, 7, and 8, key eligibility facts cannot be determined without guessing: (1) under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, we cannot verify whether the HESAWA rules (Table 5.5), Ukerewe District Council administrative formalization (p. 82), water users' registers (p. 33), ownership claims, and access-control practices (Section 7.2, p. 118) operate as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household water service access rather than cultural taboos and spring-vegetation conservation; and (2) under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2, we cannot verify Criteria 4 and 5 because none of the empirical water-access outcome tables or institutional-access analyses in Chapters 5 and 7 are present in the non-truncated text (while the only regression specified in Section 3.6 regresses household water fetched on physical distance, household size, alternative sources, and dependence). Per Hard Rule 2, decision is cannot_tell.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative mixed-methods case study (6 micro spring forest water sources across 4 villages, combining PRA, ethnographic interviews/observation, physical water and forest measurements, and a random cross-sectional survey of 180 households)
